newsitem.title: USA: Mir's new U.S. crewman marks his brithday.
newsitem.headline: Mir's new U.S. crewman marks his brithday.

text.p: Bags, boxes and birthday cake floated between shuttle Atlantis and the Mir station on Thursday as astronaut Jerry Linenger moved into his new home and celebrated his birthday.
Linenger, who was starting a four-month tour of duty on Mir, turned 42, a day after shuttle Atlantis arrived at the Russian space outpost.
Flight controllers at mission control in Houston sang "Happy Birthday" and the two crews ate a cake baked by Atlantis astronaut Marsha Ivins.

Linenger received a private call from his wife, Kathryn, who is expecting their second child in June. He hoped to be back on earth in time for the birth. Atlantis was due to return to Mir in May to bring him home.
Linenger, a Navy Captain and medical doctor, was taking the place of astronaut John Blaha, who has been aboard the station since September.
"I've had a great stay onboard the Mir space station," Blaha said in a televised interview. "But now that the shuttle is here... I'm looking forward to going home."
Blaha, who was to return to earth aboard Atlantis after 128 days in space, said he was looking forward to being reunited with his wife of 30 years, Brenda.
"We're going to have a big date," he said. "I'm going to grab hold of her and kiss her and hug her and we're going to take from there."
Linenger was to perform more than 80 experiments during his four-month stay on Mir. He also was set to become the first American to make a spacewalk from the station.
Linenger is the fourth U.S. astronaut to live and work aboard Mir as part of a NASA's effort to prepare for construction of the international space station in collaboration with Russia.
"We are continuing to learn how to work with the Russians but it is fair to say that we are over the hump," mission operations director Bob Castle said.
After five missions to Mir, the shuttle dockings had become routine, he said. "We're getting fairly good at it."
The shuttle crew had completed almost all its cargo deliveries to Mir by Thursday morning, but were still collecting items from Mir for return to earth on Atlantis.
The shuttle is due to depart Mir on Sunday night and return to earth at the Kennedy Space Centre on Wednesday.
At the launch site, officials said an initial inspection of Atlantis' twin solid rocket boosters revealed no signs of the nozzle damage that affected two recent shuttle missions.

The November launch of shuttle Columbia was delayed for a week while engineers studied the problem which caused deep grooves in the protective insulation that lines the bell-like nozzles of the booster rockets.
Atlantis's booster rockets, which peeled away from the shuttle about two minutes after launch, were recovered from the Atlantic Ocean for refurbishment and reuse.
The shuttle's left-hand booster escaped damage when one of three parachutes failed to open during Sunday's predawn launch, officials said.
